Read the transcript of the audio guide
  1. In March 1868 a twenty-nine-year-old Scot landed in San Francisco, asked a passer-by for the quickest way out of the city, and set off east on foot toward a wall of mountains he had never seen. source
  2. John Muir was born in Dunbar, Scotland, on 21 April 1838, and attended the local schools until he was eleven. source
  3. In 1849 his family emigrated to the United States and settled on Wisconsin farmland. source
  4. In 1867, working in a carriage shop in Indianapolis, a file slipped and blinded him in one eye. source
  5. When his sight came back he resolved to give up machinery and devote himself to the natural world. source
  6. He walked out across the San Joaquin Valley and up into the Sierra Nevada, which he named "the Range of Light." source
  7. Writing, for Muir, was a way of defending what he loved. source
  8. In 1890, after a campaign Muir fought alongside the editor Robert Underwood Johnson, an act of Congress created Yosemite National Park. source
  9. Two years later Muir and a circle of allies founded the Sierra Club "to do something for wildness and make the mountains glad." source
  10. President Theodore Roosevelt came west in 1903 to see Yosemite with Muir himself. source
  11. The two slipped away from the official party into the back country for several days; Roosevelt went home and threw the weight of the presidency behind protecting the nation's forests, parks and monuments. source
  12. Muir wrote: source
  13. Thousands of tired, nerve-shaken, over-civilized people are beginning to find out that going to the mountains is going home; that wildness is a necessity. source
  14. Which wild place near you would you fight to protect, and how would you persuade other people to help?
Read the transcript of the short and the video
  1. John Muir came to America from Scotland as an eleven-year-old farm boy in 1849 and grew into the most persuasive voice for keeping wild country wild. source
  2. He helped win Yosemite its national park, founded the Sierra Club, and took a president camping among the giant sequoias. source
  3. In March 1868 a twenty-nine-year-old Scot landed in San Francisco, asked a passer-by for the quickest way out of the city, and set off east on foot toward a wall of mountains he had never seen. source
  4. He walked out across the San Joaquin Valley and up into the Sierra Nevada, which he named "the Range of Light." source
  5. Writing, for Muir, was a way of defending what he loved. source
